data.title: PayPal stock falls 4% as leadership shake-up tests turnaround strategy
data.description:
PayPal stock PYPL fell 4% on Friday after the payments company announced a series of leadership changes as part of its turnaround efforts under CEO Enrique Lores.

The appointments include a new chief financial officer and executives overseeing consumer financial services, payments and artificial intelligence operations.

The company said the changes follow several months of strategic planning aimed at clarifying priorities across its core businesses, simplifying its operating model and strengthening leadership accountability.

However, the management overhaul comes as investors remain cautious about PayPal's ability to revive growth and regain market share.

PayPal has lost about 7% over the past 12 months.

The stock has also fallen approximately 82% from its all-time closing high of $308.53 reached on July 23, 2021.

PayPal appoints new CFO and business heads

Claire Bramley, currently CFO of cloud-based accounting software provider Xero, will join PayPal as executive vice president and CFO on February 1, 2027.

She will replace Jamie Miller, who has served as chief financial and operating officer.

Bramley will work with Miller during February to support the transition.

Bramley previously held senior finance positions at HP, where her tenure overlapped with Lores.

PayPal also appointed Kartik Mani as president and head of Consumer Financial Services and Venmo.

Mani joins from American Express, where he was president of Global Network and Partner Services. Venmo general manager Alexis Sowa will continue in her role and report to him.

Suzan Kereere, who currently leads PayPal's Global Markets business, will become president and head of Payment Services and Crypto.

She will succeed Jeff Pomeroy, who had been serving as interim head and will continue leading Payment Services and Platforms, reporting to Kereere.

Juan Rio will join the company on November 30 as executive vice president of AI Business Transformation and Operations.

He previously worked at Brightstar.AI as managing director and chief delivery officer. Rio will oversee AI initiatives, cost simplification and enterprise operating effectiveness.

Separately, PayPal announced that Chief Risk Officer Aaron Webster would leave the company.

Ratinder Bedi, senior vice president of Credit and Fraud Risk, will serve as interim head of the risk organisation while PayPal searches for a permanent replacement.

Board appointment and investor concerns

PayPal also appointed Brian J. Lee to its board of directors, effective November 30, 2026.

Lee served as Goldman Sachs' chief risk officer from 2019 to January 2025 and most recently chaired its Risk Council through October 2026.

The leadership changes come as Wall Street analysts remain divided over PayPal's prospects.

Of the 45 analysts covering the stock, 31 have a Hold rating, seven recommend selling, and seven have a Buy rating.

Monness Crespi Hardt analyst Gus Galá recently downgraded PayPal to Sell from Neutral and set a $48 price target.

He cited market-share losses and unfavourable business trends, including a year-over-year decline in third-quarter transaction revenue from PayPal's products and services.

Analysts at Freedom Broker, Cleveland Research and Bank of America have also recently downgraded the stock.

Analysts assess PayPal's growth engines

Not all analysts are negative on the company. Susquehanna analyst James Friedman maintains a Positive rating and a $67 price target.

Friedman believes PayPal's growth prospects should not depend entirely on its traditional branded checkout business.

He identified buy now, pay later services, Venmo, and Braintree's value-added merchant tools as three newer growth engines, each of which has recorded double-digit growth.

He argued that the traditional checkout business may only need to achieve modest growth of 2% to 3% to support overall profit expansion.

Friedman also expects PayPal to treat 2027 as an investment year, directing spending towards these three growth areas while using internal cost savings to keep overall earnings steady.

The turnaround, which Lores has led since joining in March, has focused on cost reductions and greater adoption of artificial intelligence.

PayPal's fourth-quarter results, expected in early February, will provide investors with an opportunity to assess management's progress.

Forward guidance and updates on the turnaround strategy are likely to remain central to the market's assessment of the company's new leadership team.

data.title: Why Intel shares are falling over 5% on Friday?
data.description:
Intel shares INTC fell on Friday as a broader selloff in semiconductor stocks intensified, with investors reassessing the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and the profitability of the industry.

The stock was down 5.36% by 1:06 AM ET, trading at $52.74. Intel's stock has seen a sharp dip since its earnings on Oct 29, after which it lost close to 29% in the next session.

On Friday, though, the weakness was not limited to just Intel.

Nvidia, AMD, Micron and Broadcom also declined as the technology sector faced another bout of selling. Anthropic shares, which had enjoyed a blockbuster stock market debut on Thursday, also reversed course.

The pressure on chipmakers has also spread across international markets, with Asian semiconductor stocks facing heavy losses.

For Intel, however, the broader market weakness is only part of the problem. The company is dealing with several challenges of its own, ranging from slowing PC demand and manufacturing difficulties to legal action and changes in its investor base.

Chip stocks face broader AI concerns

The latest selling comes as investors become increasingly cautious about the AI trade following weeks of volatility.

Concerns over data center spending, financing requirements and the time required to generate returns have weighed on semiconductor companies.

Nvidia's recent leadership controversy and questions surrounding its financial relationships across the AI ecosystem have added another layer of uncertainty.

Anthropic's IPO was expected to bring some relief to the struggling AI trade, but sentiment failed to improve even after the Claude maker delivered a blockbuster Nasdaq debut on Thursday.

Anthropic itself led the broader tech sector decline on Friday, falling more than 12%.

Intel has been particularly vulnerable because its turnaround depends on both recovering its traditional PC business and establishing itself as a major contract chip manufacturer.

Nvidia reduces Intel stake as PC concerns grow

A regulatory filing revealed that Nvidia reduced its Intel holding by 25% during the third quarter, cutting its reported position from 214.8 million shares to approximately 161.1 million.

Nvidia had invested $5 billion in Intel in December 2025, supporting its manufacturing ambitions. Although it retains a substantial position, the reduction has raised questions about the investment relationship.

Intel is also facing a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit filed in federal court in California.

The lawsuit, led by Michigan's City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, alleges that Intel executives failed to disclose the impact of slowing PC sales and excess inventory on the company's financial performance.

The allegations follow Intel's warning that PC demand could remain weak through the first half of 2027.

Higher memory prices and supply shortages have increased computer costs, while manufacturing bottlenecks have limited Intel's ability to meet demand for some data center processors.

The company's fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $15 billion to $16 billion also fell short of Wall Street expectations of approximately $17 billion.

Fresh layoffs add to Intel's challenges

Intel's restructuring efforts are continuing under CEO Lip-Bu Tan as the company attempts to lower costs and streamline operations.

It has begun another round of layoffs within its global information technology organization, although the number of affected employees has not been disclosed.

Intel's reported workforce has fallen by approximately 27,800 employees since the end of 2024. The company said it regularly reviews its staffing requirements to ensure resources are aligned with its business priorities.

However, even this effort has not been able to win back investors, with broader market sentiment refusing to improve.

Some good news: Intel wins new customers

Despite the pressure, Intel has secured two important customer developments that could support its manufacturing ambitions.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan announced Thursday that the company had signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P chip manufacturing process.

Intel has not disclosed the customer's identity, but the agreement marks progress in its effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

Separately, Microsoft became the first publicly named customer for Intel Foundry's EMIB advanced packaging technology, which will be used for Microsoft's Azure first-party silicon.

The companies also expanded their collaboration through multi-year agreements covering Intel Xeon processors and future Azure infrastructure.

data.title: Why Broadcom shares are down over 11% on Friday
data.description:
Broadcom shares AVGO are sliding on Friday as the broader semiconductor sector faces continued pressure.

The stock fell nearly 11.28% by 12:36 AM ET, dropping to around $307.5 in one of its sharper single-day declines in recent months.

Shares opened lower and continued to weaken as the session progressed. Broadcom has already been under pressure amid the wider AI trade selloff in recent weeks.

The stock has lost over 25% in the past six months as investors remain cautious about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and concentration risks tied to major customers.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index was down close to 9% with Nvidia on course for a seventh straight decline.

Google trims TPU shipments

Influential supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reported that Google has cut planned 2027 shipments of Broadcom-designed TPU 8i chips by approximately one million units.

This represents roughly 20% of the previously expected volume of Broadcom's chups.

The reductions are concentrated in the higher-priced 8i Max model, as per Kuo.

Kuo indicated that Google plans to offset some of the shortfall by increasing orders for MediaTek-designed alternatives.

The shift raises questions about Broadcom’s share of Google’s custom AI accelerator business and potential revenue implications for future years.

Goldman Sachs price target cut

Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider lowered the firm’s 12-month price target on Broadcom to $460 from $540 while maintaining a Buy rating.

The reduction reflected a lower valuation multiple of 25 times earnings, down from 30 times, driven by compression in peer multiples across the semiconductor sector.

The target cut, announced earlier in the week, continues to weigh on sentiment as investors reassess growth assumptions for AI-related revenue.

Before this, Rothschild & Co Redburn had also downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy, cutting its target to $398 from $595.

Broadcom reports its quarterly earnings on December 9.

Broader AI market concerns

The decline is occurring against a backdrop of ongoing headwinds for Nvidia, including legal and regulatory scrutiny, which have dampened enthusiasm across the AI ecosystem.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday.

His office is examining whether the company or former chief executive Jensen Huang allowed advanced chips to reach China and misled investors.

Nvidia's search for a permanent chief executive is another issue facing investors with Huang's exit being seen as a big headwind in the short term.

Anthropic's IPO was expected to bring some relief to the struggling AI trade, but sentiment failed to improve even after the Claude maker delivered a blockbuster Nasdaq debut on Thursday.

Anthropic itself led the broader tech sector decline on Friday, falling more than 10.5%.

data.title: Bitcoin price today: BTC falls below $60,000 for first time since July
data.description:
Bitcoin price today slipped below $60,000 on Friday, 20 November 2026, for the first time since early July. Bitcoin traded at $59,676.83, down 4.8% over 24 hours.

The fall came as record outflows from BlackRock's spot Bitcoin ETF, a sharp sell-off in US tech stocks, and the prospect of further Fed rate rises weighed on risk appetite.

What happened to Bitcoin today?

Bitcoin dropped sharply in the afternoon, sliding from $61,113 to a 24-hour low of $58,678.48.

Coinbase daily data show Bitcoin last traded below $60,000 on 2 July, when it touched $59,520.02.

The world's largest cryptocurrency is now about 53% below its record of $126,296 from 6 October 2025.

The sell-off hit the wider market.

Ether fell below $1,700 for the first time since 3 July and was at $1,654.41, down 6.4% in 24 hours, after a low of $1,622.00.

XRP was down 5.0% and Solana was down 5.5% over the same period.

Why is Bitcoin down today?

The clearest pressure is coming from US spot Bitcoin ETFs.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $541.1M of net outflows on 19 November, its largest one-day outflow on record, according to Farside Investors.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $582.3M in total on Thursday, and about $3.47 billion so far in November, Farside data show.

IBIT has posted net outflows on 13 of the month's 14 trading days.

Leverage has added to the move. CoinGlass data showed more than $700 million of crypto positions liquidated over 24 hours on Friday, mostly bets on higher prices.

Wider markets are also weak. The Nasdaq Composite was down 2.06%, as AI stocks extended their sell-off.

Rate expectations are another headwind.

Minutes of the Fed's October meeting said almost all officials judged that further rate rises would likely be appropriate.

Higher rates tend to weigh on assets such as Bitcoin that pay no yield.

Sentiment is already weak. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index read 12 ("extreme fear") on Friday.

What happens next for Bitcoin?

Bitcoin has already dipped below the 2 July low of $59,520.02, its lowest level since 1 July. The next level is $57,717.55, the 1 July low.

Bitcoin is on course for a seventh straight weekly loss on Coinbase.

A recovery back above $60,000 would ease the pressure, but ETF flows will be key.

The next big macro test is the Fed's 8-9 December meeting.

Should you buy Bitcoin now?

Bitcoin is highly volatile, and today's break below $60,000 shows how fast prices can move.

data.title: Why CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are falling on Friday?
data.description:
Shares of Nebius Group and CoreWeave fell on Friday as optimism around Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO faded amid broader concerns about the AI trade.

Nebius dropped 11.7% by 11:45 AM ET, while CoreWeave also declined 10.7%, extending recent weakness in the neocloud sector.

CoreWeave has slipped more than 30% over the last eight sessions, while Nebius has tumbled more than 40% over the same period.

The broader market also remained under pressure, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq turning negative for 2026 after yet another day in the red.

Anthropic IPO fails to lift AI trade

Anthropic's IPO was expected to bring some relief to the struggling AI trade, but sentiment failed to improve even after the Claude maker delivered a blockbuster Nasdaq debut on Thursday.

Anthropic itself led the broader tech sector decline on Friday, falling more than 10.5%.

Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius have borne the brunt of the selloff.

Their heavy debt loads have become a major point of contention among investors, especially amid tightening credit markets and rising borrowing costs.

Both CoreWeave and Nebius play a critical role in the AI trade as specialized cloud providers, often called neoclouds.

They purchase large volumes of high-end Nvidia GPUs and other chips, then rent out the computing capacity to AI labs, enterprises and researchers that need massive processing power to train and run large language models.

Burry reminds investors of his warning

Investor Michael Burry added to the pressure with a post on X stating that he had “tried to warn” investors about CoreWeave, Nebius, Nvidia and semiconductor stocks.

Burry, known for his “Big Short” call ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, noted that he had provided information that would prompt selling, even if he did not explicitly recommend shorting the stocks.

"I tried to warn you all. I didn’t say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell," Burry said.

Chipmaker scrutiny and related risks

Rising legal and regulatory scrutiny around Nvidia, including probes related to former CEO Jensen Huang and potential China-linked risks, weighed on sentiment toward the broader AI supply chain.

Nvidia is a backer of both neoclouds.

Similar concerns have extended to other chipmakers, such as AMD, which was also tumbling on Friday.

With the political climate changing and major chipmakers under scrutiny, the sustainability of the AI boom is facing growing questions.

Separately, disclosures showed that the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, Huang's charity, has committed $350 million to rent computing capacity from CoreWeave for research grants.

The arrangement, with more than $100 million already spent, has drawn attention to the close financial ties between Nvidia's ecosystem and its customers, raising questions about circular financing in the sector.

CoreWeave also came under pressure, with Bernstein reiterating its Sell rating on the stock on Wednesday.

Bernstein maintains a bearish stance on CoreWeave, setting a $54 price target on November 20, 2026, after cutting its target from $74 to $51 in late October 2026.

data.title: Michael Burry takes profits on Nvidia puts as chip stocks extend sell-off
data.description:
Michael Burry, the investor made famous by The Big Short, has taken profits on part of his bearish bets against Nvidia and the semiconductor sector following a sharp technology sell-off this week.

In a Friday update to subscribers of his Cassandra Unchained Substack, Burry said he sold 50% of his put options on Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), locking in what he described as substantial gains.

He retained the remaining half of both positions.

Put options increase in value when the underlying shares decline, allowing investors to profit from falling stock prices.

Burry also reduced some of his bullish exposure, selling roughly one-third of his call options on animal health company Zoetis (NYSE: ZTS) to secure gains.

However, he left his bearish April 2027 put options on the Nasdaq 100 untouched, maintaining his longer-term negative outlook on large-cap technology stocks.

Burry increases MercadoLibre stake

Alongside the profit-taking, Burry increased his position in Latin American e-commerce company MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI) by 20%.

He also pointed to what he described as "absolute relative strength" in several stocks, including healthcare companies Molina Healthcare (NYSE: MOH) and HCA Healthcare (NYSE: HCA), software company Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE) and grocery retailer Sprouts Farmers Market (NASDAQ: SFM).

The portfolio changes indicate that Burry is adjusting some of his positions following the recent market moves while retaining his bearish exposure to the Nasdaq 100.

His decision to lock in part of his Nvidia and semiconductor ETF gains came as chip stocks endured a difficult week, with Nvidia extending its losing streak despite reporting strong quarterly results.

Nvidia shares extend losing streak

Nvidia shares fell for a seventh consecutive session on Friday and were on track for their worst weekly performance since November 2018.

The decline came despite the chipmaker reporting record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure.

Net profit increased 109% to $64.9 billion, beating Wall Street forecasts.

Interim CEO Colette Kress also provided a strong outlook, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion and raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75%.

However, the earnings performance did little to support the stock as investors continued to assess concerns surrounding the company and the broader technology sector.

Nvidia has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving the potential diversion of advanced chips to China.

Two House Democrats reportedly opened an inquiry into whether the company sought to influence the Commerce Department's investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company suspected of illegally diverting advanced chips to China.

Separately, Representative Brett Guthrie, chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, sent a letter to Kress requesting that Nvidia officials appear before the panel by December 2.

Semiconductor sell-off weighs on technology stocks

Nvidia's decline spread across the wider semiconductor sector, adding to pressure on technology stocks as investors questioned whether substantial spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure would generate sufficient returns.

The Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, fell 9% over the week.

Other major chipmakers also recorded steep losses on Friday.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) dropped more than 11%, while Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) declined over 13%.

The declines reflected broader concerns about valuations and supply chains across the semiconductor industry.

data.title: Evening digest: Anthropic slides after record debut, Bitcoin slips below $60k
data.description:
US markets remained under pressure on Friday as Anthropic shares fell over 10% in their second trading session, adding to concerns about the artificial intelligence trade.

Bitcoin dropped below $60,000 for the first time since July as record outflows from BlackRock's spot ETF and broader risk aversion weighed on cryptocurrencies.

Gold prices slid to a 14-month low and headed for their steepest weekly decline in eight months amid expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases.

Oil prices also fell, with Brent crude on track for a third consecutive weekly decline as strong Middle Eastern exports outweighed concerns about disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Anthropic stock falls nearly 10% on second trading day

Anthropic shares extended their decline on Friday after failing to sustain the gains from their blockbuster Nasdaq debut.

The stock fell 10.52% to trade at $86.95. The stock remained slightly above its IPO price of $83.

The decline followed a volatile debut on Thursday, when Anthropic opened at $111.50, reached a high of $115.10 and closed at $97.17.

More than 846 million shares changed hands during the first session.

The weakness reflects broader concerns about AI-related investments rather than company-specific developments alone.

Investors had hoped Anthropic's record listing would restore confidence in AI stocks, which have faced pressure over the scale and profitability of data centre and chip spending.

Anthropic's underwriters exercised their option to purchase all 147 million additional shares, bringing the total offering to $93.5 billion.

The stock remained above its IPO price, but its early gains had narrowed considerably.

Bitcoin price falls below $60,000

Bitcoin dropped below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, extending a broad cryptocurrency selloff.

The largest cryptocurrency traded at $58,261, down 7.1% over 24 hours. It is now approximately 53% below its record high of $126,296 reached on October 6, 2025.

Selling pressure also affected other major cryptocurrencies.

Ether fell below $1,700 for the first time since July 3, trading at $1,604, while XRP and Solana declined 5% and 5.5%, respectively.

Outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds added to the pressure.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on November 19, its largest single-day withdrawal on record, according to Farside Investors.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs collectively lost $582.3 million that day and approximately $3.47 billion so far in November.

More than $700 million in cryptocurrency positions were liquidated over 24 hours, mostly bullish bets, according to CoinGlass.

Gold price hits 14-month low

Gold extended its decline on Friday, with spot prices falling 2.69% to $3,524.29 an ounce after touching $3,513.54, the lowest level since September 2025.

Bullion was down approximately 9.2% for the week, its steepest weekly decline since March.

US gold futures for December delivery fell 4.2% to $3,530.40 an ounce.

A stronger dollar and expectations of higher US interest rates have weighed on the precious metal.

Markets were pricing in a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

The selloff in AI-linked equities may also have prompted investors to liquidate gold positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.

Silver fell 3.6% to $41.23 an ounce, while platinum and palladium declined 2.6% and 2.1%, respectively. All four precious metals were heading for a second consecutive weekly decline.

Oil prices head for third weekly decline

Oil prices were mixed on Friday but remained on track for a third consecutive weekly decline as strong exports from the Middle East helped ease supply concerns.

Brent crude futures gained 0.22% to $92.17 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate December futures rose 0.83% to $83.90.

Brent was heading for a weekly loss of nearly 5%, while December WTI was set to fall 5.8%.

Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels, strengthening expectations of a potential supply surplus.

However, geopolitical risks remain.

The Iran-aligned Houthi movement threatened Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports after launching missile attacks on Riyadh.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy also said two oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and were burning.

The market is also monitoring OPEC+ discussions scheduled for November 29, when ministers will consider the group's 2027 output policy.

data.title: SpaceX stock slips: why its 8.26% bond yield matters
data.description:
SpaceX (SPCX) stock is inching lower on Friday after management announced a $32 billion bond sales to finance the company’s access to Nvidia’s artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

The largest slice of that deal yielded 8.259%, well above the 5.95% for the average US investment-grade bond on Thursday.

The sale gives SpaceX a way to expand its AI business without issuing new shares.

But it also puts a price on that expansion: the company is committing to years of lease payments while the revenue those chips can generate remains uncertain.

What the 8.259% yield actually tells investors

The 8.259% yield applied to about $25.2 billion of notes, the largest of three tranches.

That was 231 basis points above the broad investment-grade average and roughly 106 basis points above where SpaceX’s own 2031 corporate debt traded Thursday.

The comparisons are imperfect because the securities differ in structure and repayment terms.

Still, the pricing shows how much return investors were offered to fund this particular buildout.

And because 8.259% is the yield on one tranche, multiplying it by $32 billion would misstate the deal’s annual interest bill.

SpaceX shareholders should focus on the lease payments the company owes and how much operating cash the equipment can generate against them.

How the bond sale helps SpaceX grow without dilution

The bullish case starts with what SpaceX gets for the money.

Under its agreement with an Apollo-managed entity, the giant expects to lease Nvidia’s next-gen Vera Rubin chips and related equipment as deliveries begin in the first half of 2027.

That lets it bring more computing capacity online for Grok and cloud customers while spreading payments over roughly five years.

CFO Bret Johnsen said in October that SpaceX was seeing payback periods of less than a year on its AI infrastructure investments.

If the new capacity comes close to that pace, existing shareholders could benefit from the expansion without giving up any of their ownership to finance it.

The test is whether those returns hold as SpaceX adds capacity on a much larger scale.

Why the terms make the pullback harder to buy

The deal is positive for SpaceX’s ability to expand, but the terms tilt the stock read bearish in the near term.

The company expects roughly $40 billion in principal payments across the broader lease arrangement, and those commitments can outlast today’s pricing for AI computing.

If customers rent fewer hours than SpaceX expects, or newer chips drive down what customers will pay, the lease payments still come due.

The strongest evidence for buying the dip would be customer contracts that secure both usage and pricing, alongside cash flow figures that show what remains after power, operating costs, and lease payments.

Until then, the bond sale gives investors more reason to model those obligations than to raise their estimates for what the AI business is worth.

data.title: Anthropic IPO closes at $93.5B after full greenshoe, $119.5B with placement
data.description:
The Anthropic IPO has formally closed at $93.5 billion after underwriters bought every extra share they were allowed to, Anthropic said on 20 November 2026.

With a $26 billion private placement to seven chip and cloud groups alongside it, the total raised comes to about $119.5 billion.

The closing statement confirms 1,127,000,000 Class A shares sold at $83 each. That includes the full exercise of the underwriters' option to buy 147,000,000 additional shares from the company, the so-called greenshoe.

Anthropic IPO raise rises to $93.5 billion

When the deal priced on 18 November, the headline raise was about $81.3 billion from roughly 980 million shares. The greenshoe adds about $12.2 billion at the $83 offer price, an Invezz calculation, lifting gross proceeds to roughly $93.5 billion.

Of the 1.127 billion shares, 1,103,351,354 were sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 by existing stockholders. Anthropic received about $91.6 billion before underwriting discounts and expenses. The selling stockholders' portion, worth just under $2 billion at $83, does not go to the company.

That extends the Anthropic IPO's lead as the largest listing on record, ahead of SpaceX's debut in June. It also gives a newly public company one of the deepest cash cushions in the market as it scales up spending on computing power.

The $26bn private placement

Alongside the public offering, Anthropic closed the sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 price, for about $26.0 billion. The buyers were AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners.

Those shares were sold in a private placement and were not registered under the Securities Act. They do not form part of the Class A stock that trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Including the selling stockholders, the IPO and the placement together raised about $119.5 billion before fees. Most of the companies that bought in are also Anthropic's suppliers of chips, memory, cloud capacity or manufacturing.

Who led the deal

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were the lead book-running managers. JPMorgan, Citigroup, Barclays, Wells Fargo Securities, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, RBC Capital Markets and UBS Investment Bank were also bookrunners.

A further seven banks acted as additional bookrunners and five as co-managers. The registration statement was declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission on 18 November, and the shares began trading the following day.

What the close means for ANT investors

A fully exercised greenshoe is usually a sign of strong demand. Underwriters normally sell extra shares at the outset and use the option to cover that position, which they tend to do in full when the stock trades above the offer price.

ANT did that on day one. The stock opened at $111.50 on 19 November and closed at $97.17, about 17% above the $83 offer price. At that close, the 1.127 billion IPO shares were worth roughly $109.5 billion, an Invezz calculation, a paper gain of about $16bn for buyers in the deal.

For the strategic investors, the 313 million Class N shares were worth about $4.4 billion more at Thursday's close than they paid, on the same basis. That cushion has been tested on Friday, as ANT fell about 10% in early trading amid a wider AI selloff, covered in our Anthropic stock price report for day two.

Morningstar, which holds a $92 fair value estimate on the stock, said the capital raised, together with $132 billion of cash on the balance sheet, should allow Anthropic to meet its compute commitments even if revenue growth stalls. Those commitments are one of the biggest questions hanging over the shares.

Lock-up and what to watch next

Insiders cannot sell freely straight away. The lock-up runs until after results for the third quarter of next year, Bloomberg News reported, which limits the supply of new stock that could reach the market in the near term.

The next catalysts are Anthropic's first quarterly report as a public company and the start of research coverage from the banks that ran the deal, which are restricted from publishing for a period after the IPO. Independent firms have already set targets, as tracked in our Anthropic stock forecast and ANT price target roundup.

data.title: Nvidia stock falls for seventh day as Damodaran flags risks and $140 entry
data.description:
Nvidia stock NVDA fell 3% on Friday, extending its losing streak to seven consecutive sessions as the chipmaker faced renewed scrutiny over its China business and leadership transition.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday.

His office is examining whether the company or former chief executive Jensen Huang allowed advanced chips to reach China and misled investors.

The investigation adds to concerns surrounding the company following Huang's departure and allegations involving China.

Meanwhile, valuation expert and New York University professor Aswath Damodaran has identified $140 per share as a potential buying level, while warning that the leadership crisis and related developments could affect Nvidia's intrinsic value.

Damodaran identifies $140 as potential buying level

In a blog post, Damodaran, who is known as the 'Dean of Valuation', described Huang as a great CEO and said he would consider buying Nvidia shares if they fell below $140.

He estimated Nvidia's value at approximately $4.8 trillion and said he would seek a price around 30% below that valuation.

This would translate into a breakeven value of roughly $140 per share.

Damodaran said he had placed a limit buy order at that level and would add Nvidia back to his portfolio if the stock reached it.

However, he cautioned that the recent decline did not necessarily mean the shares had become cheap.

Nvidia's intrinsic value may have fallen because of the loss of its leader and the fallout from the controversy, he said.

Nvidia's market capitalisation has declined by more than $2 trillion to approximately $3.52 trillion since Huang first acknowledged an affair at the start of last week.

The company announced his resignation last Thursday and appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief.

China allegations remain a key risk

Damodaran identified the China-related allegations as a major uncertainty for Nvidia's valuation.

He said that if claims involving official Chinese government connections and chip sales through Asian business fronts proved true, the resulting legal and regulatory consequences could persist regardless of who leads the company.

The potential financial impact would depend on how the situation develops.

If the disruption from Huang's departure remains limited to short-term issues, including transition delays, margin pressure, and legal friction, Damodaran estimated that the impact on Nvidia's equity value could be contained to a 5% to 10% decline in most scenarios.

However, he warned that a broader strategic shift could have more significant consequences.

If Nvidia reduces its customer financing and ecosystem marketing efforts, its long-term revenue growth and margins could face greater pressure.

CEO succession adds to investor uncertainty

Nvidia's search for a permanent chief executive is another issue facing investors.

Damodaran considers Kress and other company insiders potential candidates.

However, he does not view Apple CEO Tim Cook as a suitable long-term choice for Nvidia, although he said Cook could potentially manage the company temporarily during a crisis.

He also highlighted the importance of corporate governance, arguing that even highly successful executives need appropriate oversight.

Meanwhile, Daiwa Securities reiterated its Outperform rating on Nvidia but lowered its price target to $185 from $245.

The brokerage said Nvidia's operating performance remained strong but identified two major concerns weighing on the shares: whether the scale of AI capital expenditure meant revenue and earnings growth were approaching a peak, and whether a new CEO could match Huang's leadership.

Daiwa said it did not believe Nvidia was nearing peak revenue or earnings as long as customers continued to generate returns from AI solutions.

However, the leadership question remains a significant uncertainty for investors as the company navigates its transition.
